claims.statement: Asana issues Service Accounts (SAs): long-lived tokens providing programmatic access to the API, an Enterprise tier feature that only Asana super admins can create from the admin console.

sources.supports: Similar to PATs, Service Accounts (SAs) are long-lived tokens that provide programmatic access to the API. Service Accounts are an Enterprise tier feature and can only be created by Asana super admins

claims.statement: Service Account scopes are distinct from OAuth scopes, and a Service Account must be created with the Full Permissions option to reach standard Asana API endpoints such as the Tasks API.

sources.supports: Service Account scopes are distinct from OAuth scopes. To access standard Asana API endpoints (for example, the Tasks API), select the Full Permissions option when creating the Service Account.

claims.statement: Asana states its API tokens, including service account tokens, should be treated as opaque and that token formats may change without notice; the documentation states no prefix, alphabet or length.

sources.supports: Asana API tokens should be treated as opaque. Token formats may change without notice. This applies to any Asana API tokens, including: personal access tokens, service account tokens, and both OAuth refresh tokens and access tokens.

claims.statement: Asana states that, unlike personal access tokens, Service Accounts provide complete access to all data within the Asana account, including private user data, which suits org-wide authorization, and it names the endpoints that require service accounts: the audit log, organizational exports and SCIM.

sources.supports: Unlike PATs, SAs provide complete access to all data within your Asana account, including private user data. As such, SAs are ideal if your app needs to have org-wide authorization. ... Authenticating Asana API endpoints that require service accounts. For example: Audit log, Organizational exports, SCIM

claims.statement: Asana's scopes page lists the Service Account scopes as User Provisioning (SCIM), Audit Logs, Exporting, Workspace Events and AI Studio Usage, separate from OAuth scopes, with a Full Permissions option for standard API endpoints.

sources.supports: Currently, the following scopes are supported: User Provisioning (SCIM), Audit Logs, Exporting, Workspace Events, AI Studio Usage API ... Service Account scopes are distinct from OAuth scopes.

claims.statement: Asana documents that only Service Accounts (in qualifying Enterprise tiers) can reach the audit log API endpoints and that only Service Accounts in Enterprise Domains can reach the SCIM endpoints.

sources.supports: only Service Accounts belonging to organizations on the Asana Enterprise+ tier, legacy tier Legacy Enterprise, or an Enterprise domain with the Compliance Management Add-on can access audit log API endpoints.
sources.locator: callout: Accessing audit log API endpoints

sources.supports: Only Service Accounts in Enterprise Domains can access SCIM endpoints.

claims.statement: Asana's audit log page says authentication with a Service Account's personal access token is required for the audit log endpoints and links that phrase to its personal access token page, so Asana's own wording describes a Service Account credential as a personal access token held by a service account.

sources.supports: Authentication with a Service Account's personal access token is required.
sources.locator: callout: Accessing audit log API endpoints

claims.statement: Asana's audit log event list contains an event for a change to the expiration setting of API service account tokens belonging to a workspace, and an event for a service account being created or reprovisioned, so an expiration setting for service account tokens is documented at workspace level; the pages read do not state its default or range.

sources.supports: workspace_service_account_token_expiry_changed: The expiration setting for API service account tokens belonging to the workspace was changed.
service_account_created: A service account was created or reprovisioned.

claims.statement: Asana's personal access token page says personal access tokens are used like OAuth access tokens, passed in the Authorization header; no page read shows a request example for a Service Account token.

sources.supports: Personal access tokens should be used similarly to OAuth access tokens when accessing the API (i.e., passing them in the Authorization header).

openQuestions.question: Candidate is not researched beyond existence: the format (prefix, alphabet, length, checksum) is not recorded and has not been researched by research-family.

The authentication page calls a Service Account token "similar to" a PAT. The documentation does not say whether a service account token is distinguishable from a PAT by any string property. If neither is, this candidate and asana:personal-access-token may be one family with two issuance contexts; kept as two because Asana documents different holders, issuers and handling rules.

No page read shows a request example for a Service Account token. The Authorization header is documented for personal access tokens and OAuth access tokens, and the audit log page calls the audit credential a Service Account's personal access token, so the same Authorization header for a Service Account token is an inference, not recorded as a claim. A provider request example for a Service Account would settle it.

Asana documents a Service Account token's issuer (an Enterprise super admin in the admin console), privilege (org-wide, scope-limited) and holder (a service account) but states no string property that separates it from a personal access token; it says all Asana API tokens are opaque and may change format. The evidence supports a distinct role over a shared opaque carrier, not a distinct grammar. An Asana statement of a format difference, or an issued sample under a maintainer's authority (issuance-gated), would settle it.

Whether a Service Account token is shown once at creation, how it is rotated or revoked, and its default expiry are not established: the Asana Help Center page that the authentication page links for service accounts is client-rendered and returned no readable text to a raw fetch on 2026-10-06. Which Asana page states it, if any, would settle it.

On 2026-10-06 the rule and detector names (not their contents) of two open-source scanner repositories were listed: Gitleaks config/gitleaks.toml at b58d3f102cf3a2c84cb7f923d05c25c9b1aed84b and TruffleHog pkg/detectors at 0186870afd2c4a90def791d80260923ba583d076. Gitleaks lists asana-client-id and asana-client-secret; TruffleHog lists asanaoauth and asanapersonalaccesstoken; none names a service account token. This is a negative observation of names only; it is not a source, not corroboration and not an expectation basis.
